Every other row of nodes is shifted half a step, each node joins its neighbors in its own row and the two nodes touching it in the next row, and all the faces are triangles." width="100%"} Creates a strip of `rows` rows with `cols` triangles in each, the same lattice as NetworkX's `triangular_lattice_graph(rows, cols)`. The nodes sit in `rows + 1` rows of `(cols + 1) // 2 + 1`, with every other row shifted half a step to the right (when `cols` is odd, the shifted rows have one node fewer so that every row of triangles ends cleanly). Each node is joined to the nodes beside it in its row and to the two nodes touching it in each neighboring row. All the bounded faces are triangles, interior nodes have degree `6`, and the lattice has `rows * cols` triangles. Each node is labelled with its zero-based position as `"(row,col)"`, and nodes are created row by row; rows `1`, `3`, ... are the shifted ones. In a directed graph every edge points to the right within a row or to the next row. The lattice is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Triangular lattices are useful for: - modeling close-packed arrangements: atoms in a crystal plane, cells in a tissue, or antenna placements - spatial simulations that need six equally spaced neighbors (percolation, epidemic spread, and Ising-type models) - test cases for planar graph algorithms, with many triangles and a high clustering coefficient ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [rows]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of rows of triangles. Must be at least `1`. [cols]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of triangles in each row, counting those pointing up and those pointing down. Must be at least `1`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each node is labelled with its position as `"(row,col)"`. Because these labels don't depend on the existing nodes, adding a second labelled lattice raises `ValueError` (labels are unique); pass `label=False` for the second one. If `False`, nodes are created without labels. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `rows=` or `cols=` is less than `1`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two rows of four triangles need three rows of three nodes, and the `2 * 4 = 8` triangles share edges, leaving `16` edges in all: ::: {#b6705345 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_triangular_lattice_graph(rows=2, cols=4) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges(), len(graph.list_triangles()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (9, 16, 8) ``` ::: ::: In a larger lattice, an interior node such as `"(2,2)"` has six neighbors, two in its own row and two in each neighboring row: ::: {#3564c728 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} lattice = ec.Graph().add_triangular_lattice_graph(rows=4, cols=8) sorted(lattice.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in lattice.neighbors("(2,2)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['(1,1)', '(1,2)', '(2,1)', '(2,3)', '(3,1)', '(3,2)'] ``` ::: :::
